content: Mesalamine is a medication prescribed to treat ulcerative colitis, a condition characterized by inflammation or erosion of the lining of the colon. Delayed-release tablets and controlled-release capsules of mesalamine are used to treat inflammation affecting any part of the colon. Suppositories and enemas, however, are specifically intended for inflammation in the lower part of the colon. Mesalamine belongs to a class of drugs known as anti-inflammatory agents, and it works by inhibiting the production of certain substances in the body that cause pain and inflammation. Mesalamine is available in several forms: delayed-release tablets, controlled-release capsules (both taken orally), and rectal formulations such as suppositories and enemas. The delayed-release tablets are typically taken three times a day, while the controlled-release capsules are taken four times a day. Suppositories are usually used one to three times daily, and enemas are generally administered once daily at bedtime. It is crucial to follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take or use mesalamine exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency. Swallow the tablets whole without splitting, chewing, or crushing them, as this could compromise the protective coating. If swallowing capsules is difficult, you may open them and mix the contents with water, stirring and drinking the mixture immediately. Do not store the mixture for later use. Rectal formulations, such as enemas and suppositories, are for rectal use only. You should begin to notice improvement within the first few days or weeks of treatment. Continue using mesalamine for the full duration of your prescription, even if you feel better early in the treatment. Do not stop taking or using mesalamine without consulting your doctor. Be aware that mesalamine suppositories and enemas may stain clothing, flooring, or other surfaces, so take precautions to avoid staining. For enemas, follow these steps: 1. Attempt to have a bowel movement before use, as the medication works best when the bowels are empty. 2. Use scissors to cut the seal of the protective foil pouch containing the bottles of medication. Avoid squeezing or cutting the bottles. Remove one bottle from the pouch. 3. Inspect the liquid inside the bottle, which should be off-white or tan in color. Slight darkening is acceptable, but do not use the liquid if it has turned dark brown. 4. Shake the bottle well to ensure the medication is mixed. 5. Remove the protective cover from the applicator tip, holding the bottle by the neck to prevent leakage. 6. Lie on your left side with your left leg straight and your right leg bent toward your chest, or kneel on a bed with your upper chest and one arm resting on the bed. 7. Gently insert the applicator tip into your rectum, pointing it slightly toward your navel. If insertion causes pain or irritation, apply a small amount of personal lubricating jelly or petroleum jelly to the tip before inserting. 8. Hold the bottle firmly, tilt it slightly, and squeeze slowly and steadily to release the medication. 9. Withdraw the applicator and remain in the same position for at least 30 minutes to allow the medication to spread through your intestine. Try to retain the medication for about 8 hours (e.g., while sleeping). Each bottle contains a single dose and should not be reused. For suppositories, follow these steps: 1. Attempt to have a bowel movement before use, as the medication works best when the bowels are empty. 2. Separate one suppository from the strip and peel off the plastic wrapper while handling it as little as possible to avoid melting it with the heat of your hands. 3. You may apply a small amount of personal lubricant or petroleum jelly to the tip of the suppository to facilitate insertion. 4. Lie on your left side and raise your right knee to your chest (or lie on your right side and raise your left knee if left-handed). 5. Using your finger, insert the suppository into your rectum, pointed end first, applying gentle pressure to insert it completely. 6. Try to keep the suppository in place for 1–3 hours or longer if possible. 7. Wash your hands thoroughly before resuming normal activities. If you are using mesalamine enemas or suppositories, ask your pharmacist or doctor for the manufacturer’s patient information for additional guidance. Mesalamine may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using mesalamine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to mesalamine, balsalazide, olsalazine, salicylates (e.g., aspirin), sulfasalazine, or any other medications. If you are using mesalamine enemas, notify your doctor if you are allergic to sulfites, foods, dyes, or preservatives. Additionally, disclose any allergies to the ingredients in the specific type of mesalamine you will be using. Your pharmacist can provide a list of ingredients. Inform your doctor and pharmacist about all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Mention medications such as aspirin, NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), digoxin, or other ulcerative colitis treatments (e.g., balsalazide, olsalazine, sulfasalazine). Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Notify your doctor if you have or have ever had pancreatitis, pericarditis, liver or kidney disease, asthma, or allergies. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking mesalamine, contact your doctor immediately. Be aware that mesalamine may cause a serious reaction, with symptoms resembling those of ulcerative colitis. Contact your doctor if you experience stomach pain, bloody diarrhea, fever, headache, weakness, rash, or red, irritated eyes. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while using mesalamine. If you miss a dose, take or use it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take or use a double dose to make up for a missed one. Mesalamine may cause side effects. Minor side effects include headache, muscle or joint pain, back pain, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, burping, constipation, gas, dry mouth, sore throat, cough, flu-like symptoms, nasal congestion, ear pain, anxiety, sweating, hemorrhoids, rectal pain, difficulty sleeping, acne, or slight hair loss. Notify your doctor if these symptoms are severe or persistent. Serious side effects include chest pain, shortness of breath, black or tarry stools, bloody vomit, vomit resembling coffee grounds, changes in urination, blood in urine, confusion, or swelling of any body part. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience these symptoms. Store mesalamine in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat, light, and moisture. Suppositories may be refrigerated but not frozen. Use all enema bottles promptly after opening the foil package. Dispose of outdated or unused medication properly, consulting your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or is not breathing. If you are taking delayed-release tablets, you may notice the tablet shell in your stool. Inform your doctor if this occurs frequently. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory, as certain tests may be required before and during treatment. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist with any questions about refilling your prescription.
